newsitem.title: USA: U.S. shuttle blasts off safely on science mission.
newsitem.headline: U.S. shuttle blasts off safely on science mission.

text.p: The space shuttle Columbia, spurting fire and smoke, soared off its Florida launch pad on Friday into a clear, blue sky, headed for a 16-day science mission.

Columbia, the oldest of NASA's four orbiters, lifted off from the Kennedy Space Centre on Florida's east coast at 2:20 p.m. EST (1920 GMT), 20 minutes late because of a problem sealing the shuttle's cabin.
"Enjoy your on-orbit 'spring break'," NASA test director John Guidi, told the seven astronauts shortly before blastoff, referring to the traditional U.S. college and school holiday.

The holiday brought tens of thousands of extra spectators out to line the roads around the Florida spaceport. Kennedy Space Centre officials were forced to turn cars away when the official viewing sites filled up two hours before the blastoff.
NASA officials also attributed the larger crowds to the rare afternoon launch. Most shuttles blast off in the early hours of the morning or soon after sunrise.

Aboard Columbia was Jim Halsell, mission commander and a veteran of two previous shuttle flights. His pilot, Susan Still, making her first flight, was only the second woman to take the shuttle's pilot's seat.
Janice Voss, the payload commander, was responsible for overseeing the mission's research programme. The mission specialists were Mike Gernhardt and Donald Thomas.
Joining the NASA astronauts were two guest scientists specialising in microgravity research, Roger Crouch and Greg Linteris.

During their 16 days aloft, the astronauts were scheduled to work around the clock in two shifts in a laboratory module mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay. They planned to light more than 200 fires in a specially designed chamber to learn more about how flames behave in space and on the earth.
"Fire has been with mankind for God knows how long, but from a scientific point of view we don't understand fire as well as we should," Halsell said.
A fire in February, which filled the Mir space station with choking black smoke, highlighted the dangers of fire aboard a spacecraft.
Other experiments would attempt to determine the structure of proteins associated with various diseases and develop new, stronger materials.

Columbia's launch was running a day late because engineers had to install thermal insulation missing from pipes in the shuttle's cooling system, a problem that may have gone undetected for more than 13 years.
The shuttle was due back to earth April 20.
